title: The Future Role of Teachers: From Instructor to Guide
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Prompted by conversations with Carl Hendrick about Alpha School's AI-driven '2 Hour Learning' model, Hughes argues that as AI handles more personalised instruction, the teacher's identity must shift from content deliverer to learning coach, motivator and project facilitator. Drawing on self-regulated learning research (Zimmerman; Dignath), self-determination theory (Ryan and Deci) and teacher-student relationship research (Roorda et al.), she argues future teachers need explicit training in coaching routines, autonomy-supportive teaching behaviours and relationship-building rather than assuming these emerge naturally. She also draws on project-based learning research (Thomas; Zhang and Ma) to argue school time can be rebalanced toward projects and applied problem-solving as AI takes on more core academic instruction. She closes by proposing a three-part reimagined teacher training model - coaching learning, mentoring motivation, facilitating applied learning - built on the same developmental, practice-based model teachers would use with students.
points: Hughes's central claim is that AI does not make teachers obsolete but repositions them as 'designers of conditions for growth' rather than sole sources of explanation.
She grounds the 'Guide' role in established research (self-regulated learning, self-determination theory, teacher-student relationship meta-analyses) rather than treating it as speculative futurism.
Her three-part reimagined teacher training model - coaching learning, mentoring motivation, facilitating applied learning - offers a concrete curriculum structure, not just a philosophical shift.
She explicitly signals ambivalence about the model ('I'm not sure whether I'm entirely comfortable with a lot of it'), distinguishing exploratory thinking from firm advocacy.
quotes: In Alpha's model, the adult in the room is reframed less as a traditional lecturer and more as a Guide. The software handles much of the personalised instruction, pacing, practice, and immediate feedback. The adult's job is not mainly to deliver whole-class lessons.

Zimmerman describes self-regulated learners as students who can set goals, manage time, use strategies, self-evaluate, seek help, and maintain motivation. Dignath and colleagues' meta-analysis found that self-regulated learning training can improve academic achievement.

Ryan and Deci argue that motivation and healthy development depend on three core psychological needs: autonomy, competence, and relatedness. When these needs are supported, students are more likely to become self-motivated and engaged.
Roorda and colleagues' meta-analysis found that affective teacher-student relationships are associated with student engagement and achievement, with especially strong links to engagement.
The future teacher is not made obsolete by AI. The future teacher is liberated from being the only source of explanation and repositioned as the designer of conditions for growth.
